value: ABR thresholds about 40 dB SPL from 1.0 to 3.5 kHz, about 45 dB SPL at 4 kHz and about 46 dB SPL at 0.8 kHz
method: auditory brainstem response to tone bursts, 0.2 to 7.0 kHz at 30 to 70 dB SPL in 5 dB steps (1 ms cos2 ramps, 3 ms plateau), subcutaneous needle electrodes, sodium pentobarbital anaesthesia, soundproof chamber
conditions: 12 geckos (7 males, 5 females) were used for the hearing tests (Methods, paraphrased from page summary); thresholds are read from the Fig 4 curve as approximate values (~) and background noise level is not reported; thresholds were significantly affected by frequency (F12,132 = 91.091, p < 0.001); the same Results paragraph says: 'Thresholds increased significantly above 4.0 kHz, particularly from 5.0 to 7.0 kHz, where 20 dB SPL increments were observed.' and 'In addition, the geckos were relatively more sensitive within another narrow band (~0.4 kHz, ~42 dB SPL).'; the Discussion narrows best sensitivity to 3.0-3.5 kHz ('a narrow range of best frequency sensitivity can be identified at 3.0-3.5 kHz'); ABR is a neural-response threshold, not a behavioural audiogram; calls of the species are quiet (dominant frequencies about 2.47-4.17 kHz, mean 3.35 kHz) per the abstract

value: attraction to light depended on light colour and decreased with increasing wavelength
method: laboratory choice chamber (rectangular arena 0.5 x 1 x 0.5 m, wooden floor, screen walls, glass ceiling) with two dead-end side tunnels that could be lit by LEDs; insects placed in the middle at dusk in a paper refuge and videotaped until morning
conditions: white (about 400 to 750 nm), blue (430 nm), green (500 nm), yellow (590 nm) and red (630 nm) LEDs were assessed, 5 to 30 individuals per experiment, adult males and females and fifth-stage nymphs, starved 10 to 25 days at 24 +/- 2 C (starvation and temperature from a page summary, paraphrased); the light position was switched from one tunnel to the other between experiments and control experiments were run without light; adult males and females did not differ in response to wavelength, both being strongly attracted to blue, and the Results state: 'Thus, yellow light was barely attractive while red light was not attractive at all.'; nymph attraction to white light was limited and not significant (P = 0.21); the text gives no replicate counts per colour (sample sizes appear only in a figure) and the green light is listed in Methods but its result is not reported in the text; red is 630 nm in Methods and 625 nm in the Results text; the Discussion calls this suggestive of some colour vision and says more tests would be needed to determine colour discrimination (paraphrase of a longer sentence); intensity held constant per the Discussion; the same paper's field survey relates house infestation to public lights (infested houses 18.0 +/- 0.6 m versus 22.6 +/- 0.4 m from a public light) and is not part of this record

method: two-choice bioassay of attraction to light transmitted through clear, yellow, green and blue filters, each with and without a UV-blocking filter; insects released and captured on sticky targets
conditions: each trial averaged about 38 psyllids and each comparison was repeated 14 times (Methods, from a page summary); filter positions left versus right were alternated between trials, psyllids were dark-adapted 15 minutes, sex was pooled after no difference between sexes, and two identical clear targets showed no positional bias (t = -0.66, df = 26, P = 0.52); the UV-blocking filter cut total intensity by 19% (9% between 400 and 700 nm); yellow was also tested with neutral density filters; with UV blocked from both targets, responses to yellow and green were equivalent despite twice the light intensity through yellow (t = -0.89, df = 26, P = 0.38); the abstract sentence 'However, attraction to blue targets was unaffected by UV light.' follows the quoted one; broadband filters differ in intensity as well as hue, so this is a behavioural preference and not a spectral-sensitivity measurement

method: Y-tube choice assay (arms 200 mm long, 40 mm diameter, opaque, each arm ending in a 40 mm sticky trap with an LED 10 mm away); one arm carried the test wavelength and the other a white LED (5000 K) as control; about 30 adults per replicate placed in the central chamber for one hour at 25 C
conditions: ten wavelengths tested, each assay replicated five times (Methods lists 365, 385, 395, 405, 415, 425, 445, 495, 525 and 590 nm while the Results give 595 nm for the longest, a discrepancy in the paper); adults were purchased commercially and held at 25 C for about 1 h before testing, and sex, age and starvation are not reported; light intensity is not reported and the paper does not say whether light sides were switched or randomised; attraction rate is insects on the trap divided by the number released, with insects left in the central chamber counted as non-responders, so the 73.5% is not a share of responders; the control (white LED) arm is scored separately and the Results state that attraction rates to the control LED were >50% at 495, 525 and 595 nm; data arcsine-transformed, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's test (alpha 0.05), ANOVA significant for test LED, non-response and control LED (all P < 0.001); in the paper's other assay the whitefly Bemisia tabaci was also attracted to 385 nm (not part of this record); ranking of the five most attractive wavelengths (385, 365, 445, 395, 405 nm) and the sample size derived as about 1,500 insects are paraphrase and arithmetic from a page summary
